title: The three births — conception, birth, and death as birth (2.1)
hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying

segments.voice: Yesterday: vidriti, the door at the top of the head, where the self came in and said, I have seen this.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. Ask a family and it gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families there's a day after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya's second chapter counts births too. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, like a part of her own body, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and in caring for the child, the text says, he cares for himself, for so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old, and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Death isn't the opposite of birth here. It's the next one. Then the chapter turns to a seer. It quotes a verse from the Rig Veda in the voice of the sage Vamadeva: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. Knowing this, the text says, Vamadeva rose up from the body and reached immortality. Notice what it honors along the way: the mother is to be nourished. Even in a list of births, it stops to say who needs care.
screen: `THE FIRST BIRTH: IN THE FATHER.` · `THE SECOND: FROM THE MOTHER.` · `THE THIRD: DEPARTING, BORN AGAIN.` · `VAMADEVA, BREAKING OUT LIKE A HAWK.` · then, large: `THREE BIRTHS.`

segments.voice: Let one breath go to the people who carried you before you were born, whoever held the hope of you, and one to those who fed and held you before you could thank them. Then, gently, think of someone who has died; in the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are.

Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.
Your line: three births. Tomorrow, the Aitareya's last chapter asks who the self is. That's day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

Birth from the mother, then growing up, then old age, the last one.

chat.meaning: The first birth is in the father, the second is the child born from the mother, and the third comes when a parent departs and is born again.

Vamadeva.meaning: a Rig Veda seer who knew the gods' births from the womb

Rig Veda.meaning: the oldest of the four Vedas

Aitareya.meaning: a short Upanishad of the Rig Veda

notes: Aitareya 2.1–4 paraphrased from memory, including 'she doesn't harm it' (na himsati) and 'she is to be nourished' (sa bhavayitri bhavayitavya bhavati). Confirm.
Verse numbering: the Aitareya's second chapter is often printed as one section (2.1) with sub-verses 1–6; the Vamadeva verse is cited as 2.5 here. Confirm.
The text's account is framed around the father; the script keeps that while giving the mother's verse its weight. A Keeper may want to frame this more.
The fork's distractor 'initiation' alludes to the separate idea of the twice-born (upanayana), not taught here.
